IAPP NEWS 

New AI model sparks alarm as governments brace for AI-driven cyberattacks

Questions are swirling as to how cybersecurity practices will remain resilient in the face of evolving AI models. Anthropic's Claude Mythos model is thrusting the issue into the spotlight, with governments and stakeholders worldwide contemplating how the new frontier model capabilities could be exploited by threat actors. IAPP Staff Writer Lexie White reports on the Mythos dilemma and other developments among major AI providers.
Full story

IAPP PODCAST

Social media's impact on children's neurological development: A conversation with Alyson Stoner

Ahead of their keynote speech at the IAPP Global Summit, author and mental health advocate Alyson Stoner sat down with IAPP Editorial Director Jedidiah Bracy to unpack what social media and emerging AI systems are doing to children's developing brains and why current tech design is not built with kids in mind. Drawing from neuroscience as well as lived experience as a child star, Stoner shares perspective on how addictive design leads to rising mental health risks and offers a message to parents, policymakers and technologists on the need for better design that takes into account children's neurological development.
Full story

ANALYSIS

Nigeria moves toward comprehensive AI regulation 

Since the EU adopted the AI Act in 2024, several African countries, including Nigeria, have been building momentum toward passing their own comprehensive AI legislation, Tech Hive Advisory Tech Policy Analyst Victoria Adaramola, CIPP/E, CIPM, FIP, writes. Beginning in 2021, Adaramola traces Nigeria's recent history of legislative proposals for AI regulations, such as the release of its National AI Strategy in 2024 and the 2025 introduction of the National Artificial Intelligence Commission (Establishment) Bill, which proposes to create a National AI Commission. She also provides several recommendations for what AI governance professionals should be monitoring in Nigeria going forward, in terms of regulatory developments.

LAW & REGULATION—U.S.

Maine's comprehensive privacy bill fails on final House vote

The Maine Legislature will not finalize comprehensive privacy legislation before the end of its current legislative session 15 April, the Maine Morning Star reports. The House voted against concurrence on Legislative Document 1822, the Maine Online Data Privacy Act, for the second time in a week, ultimately ending the bill's consideration during the current session. The House and Senate had been debating a controversial political organizations exemption before local industry groups made a final lobbying push to sway a majority of House lawmakers against the bill.

INCIDENT MANAGEMENT—SOUTH KOREA

South Korea's PIPC announces new data protection certification measures

South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission announced measures to strengthen the country's Information Security and Personal Information Protection Management System certification following recent cyberattacks on telecommunications companies and e-commerce websites. Measures include instituting a mandatory personal information protection certification on "large-scale personal information processors with significant public impact," and requiring ISMS-P certification, based on the International Standards Organization's 27001 and 27701, for critical personal information processing systems in both the public and private sectors.

CUSTOMER TRUST & EXPECTATIONS

'Transparency Hub' aims to make social media policy documents more accessible

Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society created the open-access "Transparency Hub" that aims to help the public and researchers easily find and review social media companies' privacy notices, terms of service, community standards and other platform policy documents. The Transparency Hub also has an embedded tool that allows users to review how companies' policy documents have changed over time. The goal of the project is to assist people to learn what rights they retain and what rights they lose when they sign up for social media accounts.
Full story

ENFORCEMENT—U.K.

UK DSIT to make changes to enterprise-connected device code of practice

The U.K. Department for Science, Innovation and Technology will modify its proposed code of practice for enterprise-connected device security, and potentially add additional policy measures in the form of regulation, certification and other assurance mechanisms following a public consultation. According to responses from the consultation, 95% of respondents said the U.K. government should do more to intervene to protect the security of such products. Additionally, 76% said the cyber risks posed to enterprise-connected devices are distinct from other connect devices, which necessitates a separate code of practice.
